illustrious.path: Latin illustris meant lit up, bright, from lustrare, to illuminate. A brilliant, shining reputation gave illustrious its sense of someone made famous and highly distinguished.

imbibe.path: Latin imbibere meant to drink in. The literal sense of taking in liquid extended naturally to taking in ideas, so imbibe covers both drinking a beverage and absorbing knowledge.

imbroglio.path: Italian imbrogliare meant to entangle or confuse, related to French brouiller, to mix up. An imbroglio is a situation so tangled it becomes an embarrassing mess to sort out.

imbue.path: Latin imbuere meant to wet or soak thoroughly. Soaking a material with liquid became a figure for saturating a person or thing with a quality, belief, or feeling.

immaculate.path: Latin immaculatus meant without stain or blemish. Immaculate kept that sense exactly: completely clean, without a single mark or flaw.

immaterial.path: Latin materia meant matter or substance. Something immaterial literally has no physical substance, and by extension, a fact with no bearing on a matter is dismissed as immaterial, beside the point.

imminent.path: Latin imminere meant to overhang or threaten from above, as a cliff looms over a path. Something looming overhead in that way is imminent: about to happen at any moment.

immure.path: Latin immurare meant to enclose within walls. Immure kept that literal sense of being shut in by walls, whether a real prison or any confining, isolating situation.

immutable.path: Latin immutabilis meant unchangeable, from mutare, to change. Immutable describes whatever is fixed beyond the reach of change, whether a law of nature or a firm rule.

impair.path: Latin pejorare meant to make worse, from pejor, worse. Impair kept that exact sense: to weaken or damage something's condition or function.

impart.path: Latin impartire meant to share out, give a portion of something. To impart knowledge or a quality is to give someone a share of it, passing it from oneself to another.

impartial.path: Latin pars meant a part or side. Someone impartial refuses to take a part, a side, in a dispute, weighing all sides fairly instead.

impasse.path: French impasse named a dead-end street, one that cannot be passed through. The word extended from a blocked street to any deadlock or negotiation with no way forward.

impassive.path: Latin passivus meant capable of feeling or suffering, from pati, to feel. Impassive describes a face or manner showing none of that feeling, betraying no emotion at all.

impeccable.path: Latin impeccabilis meant incapable of sin, unable to err, from peccare, to sin or make a mistake. Impeccable narrowed from moral perfection to any performance so flawless it is beyond criticism.

impecunious.path: Latin pecunia meant money, originally wealth measured in cattle, from pecu, livestock. Impecunious describes someone plainly lacking that money, having little or none to their name.

impede.path: Latin impedire meant to shackle the feet, entangling someone so they cannot walk freely. Tripping up a person's feet gave impede its sense of obstructing progress of any kind.

impediment.path: From the same root as impede, an impediment is the noun for whatever shackles the feet, literally or figuratively: an obstacle that trips up progress.

impel.path: Latin impellere meant to drive or push forward into motion. Impel kept that force of a push, whether physical or the inner push of a motive that drives someone to act.

impending.path: Latin impendere meant to hang over, overhang threateningly. Something impending hangs suspended just above the present moment, usually an unwelcome event about to fall.

impenetrable.path: Latin penetrare meant to enter deeply into. Impenetrable describes whatever resists that entry, whether a physical barrier that cannot be passed through or an idea too dense to understand.

imperil.path: Latin periculum meant danger or risk. To imperil something is literally to bring it into that danger, putting it at risk of harm.

imperious.path: Latin imperiosus meant commanding, powerful, from imperium, supreme power, from imperare, to command. Imperious describes someone who issues commands with the arrogant confidence of a ruler.

impermeable.literal: not able to be passed through
impermeable.path: Latin permeare meant to pass through, from meare, to go. Impermeable describes a material that blocks that passage entirely, letting nothing through, whether water, gas, or light.

impertinent.path: Latin pertinere meant to belong to, relate to, from tenere, to hold. Something impertinent does not hold to what is relevant, and a person who is impertinent oversteps the bounds of what is fitting, rudely.

imperturbable.path: Latin turbare meant to throw into disorder, from turba, crowd, commotion. Imperturbable describes a calm that no amount of disorder or upset can shake.

impervious.path: Latin pervius meant passable, having a way through, from via, road. Impervious describes a surface or a person that gives nothing a way in, whether water or an argument meant to change their mind.

impetuous.path: Latin impetus meant a violent rushing attack, from petere, to seek or rush at. Impetuous describes acting with that same headlong rush, driven by sudden impulse rather than careful thought.
